newsitem.title: UK: BAA plans duty free expansion with DFI bid.
newsitem.headline: BAA plans duty free expansion with DFI bid.

text.p: Britain's BAA Plc, which operates seven UK airports including London Heathrow and Gatwick, said on Thursday that it was expanding its duty free business by buying U.S. company Duty Free International (DFI).

In its first major acquisition in eight years, BAA made an agreed $24 per share offer for DFI, which values the fifth largest duty and tax free business in the world at $674 million (406 million pounds).

The merger would make BAA's duty and tax free business the second largest in the world after Duty Free Shoppers (DFS), which is owned by French drink and luxury goods group LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton.

"We are trying to grow and become a global player in the world duty free market and we would like to continue growing both organically and perhaps by further joint ventures or acquisitions," finance director Russell Walls told Reuters.
Walls said, however, that the company had no specific acquisition plans at present.

DFI operates 175 stores and serves 14 international U.S. airports. Its five divisions comprise airport retailing, inflight duty free, Canadian and Mexican border duty free stores and a diplomatic/wholesale service.

"By acquiring another large business unaffected by the possible loss of European duty free, we will be able to protect and enhance profits, bring improved merchandising to DFI, build on a range of synergies, and further develop the business through a growing number of international airports," said BAA's chief executive John Egan.
BAA is funding the acquisition from existing resources and does not expect the purchase to have any short term material dulution on its earnings.
Walls said the purchase would probably enhance BAA earnings "reasonably quickly".
The company had acceptance and an option to buy new shares at the offer price for around 43 percent of DFI's fully diluted share capital.

Shares in BAA had climbed 12-1/2 pence to 585 by 1015 GMT as traders said they were buoyed by 3-1/2 pence by a lighter than expected windfall tax on the company unveiled in the British budget on Wednesday.
